You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- Test context
  - The test sets up BracketingNthOrderBrentSolver with very tight tolerances (relative 1e-12, absolute 1e-10, function value 1e-22) and maximal order 5, and solves for f(x) = (2x + 1) / (1e9 (x + 1)) on [-0.9999999, 30] with start = 15 and AllowedSolution.RIGHT_SIDE.
  - The function has a vertical asymptote at x = -1 and a root at x = -0.5. At the initial points, y(min) ≈ -0.01, y(start) ≈ 1.94e-9, so the initial bracket is [min, start] with a large discrepancy in |y| across the ends.

- How the solver proceeds
  - The main loop is in BracketingNthOrderBrentSolver.doSolve():
    - Initial bracketing: xA = min, yA ≈ -0.01; xB = start, yB ≈ +1.9e-9 (lines 197–206, 167–192).
    - Aging counters start at 0 (lines 201, 205).
    - With balanced aging, targetY = 0 (lines 231–242).
    - Using inverse polynomial interpolation (here, linear in y with 2 points), guessX computes nextX from targetY via a linear mapping in y (guessX at lines 361–380). Because |yB| << |yA| and targetY = 0, the fraction (targetY - yA)/(yB - yA) ≈ 1, so nextX lies extremely close to xB.
    - Evaluate nextY at nextX: still positive and tiny (since the true root is at -0.5 and we’re near x ≈ 15). Update logic (lines 322–341) detects nextY * yA <= 0 and updates the high bracket: xB ← nextX, increments agingA, resets agingB.

  - Aging compensation triggers
    - After two consecutive updates to xB, agingA >= MAXIMAL_AGING (2) (line 54).
    - The solver tries to “compensate” by choosing a non-zero target (lines 231–242):
      - If agingA >= 2, targetY = -REDUCTION_FACTOR * yB with REDUCTION_FACTOR = 1/16 (lines 233–236 and 57).
      - Since yB is already very small (≈ 1e-9), targetY becomes an even smaller negative (≈ -6e-11).

  - Why compensation fails
    - With targetY extremely close to zero and |yA| ≫ |yB|, the inverse interpolation in guessX again maps targetY to an x extremely close to xB (linear-in-y mapping between (yA, xA) and (yB, xB)). This is inherent to the formula in guessX (lines 361–380).
    - Evaluating the actual function near xB yields a small positive value (the function is positive for x > -0.5), so the sign with yA remains opposite and the update again replaces xB (lines 322–341), incrementing agingA further.
    - Thus, despite the aging logic, the solver keeps updating the same boundary (xB) with minuscule changes because the chosen target is too close to zero. The bracket shrinks only imperceptibly and remains far from the root near -0.5.

- Consequence
  - The loop continues updating xB with negligible progress toward satisfying either the x-interval tolerance (lines 210–229) or the function value tolerance because absYA ≈ 0.01 remains large.
  - With AllowedSolution.RIGHT_SIDE, the algorithm would return xB upon convergence, but convergence is not reached within the provided evaluation budget, leading to exceeding the maximum number of evaluations in testIssue716.

- Root cause
  - The aging compensation strategy in doSolve (lines 231–242), specifically setting targetY to a small multiple of the already tiny y on the frequently updated side (±REDUCTION_FACTOR * yB or yA), can select a target too close to zero.
  - Given large |y|-asymmetry across the bracket (|yB| ≪ |yA|), the inverse interpolation step systematically predicts points extremely close to the same boundary, ensuring the same bracket gets updated repeatedly and preventing effective rebalancing.
  - This matches the bug report: the solver “attempts to balance the bracketing points by targeting a non-zero value instead of the real root,” but “the chosen target is too close to zero,” so the inverse approximation “is always on the same side,” causing repeated updates to the same bracket and exceeding max iterations.

Where it shows in code:
- Aging logic and target selection: doSolve at lines 231–242; MAXIMAL_AGING (line 54); REDUCTION_FACTOR (line 57).
- Inverse interpolation that maps targetY to nextX: guessX at lines 361–380.
- Repeated update of the same boundary and aging counters: doSolve at lines 322–341.

In short: When one side becomes “aged,” the solver’s compensation target is scaled by the tiny y-value of the opposite side, making the target effectively zero. With highly asymmetric |y|, the inverse interpolation keeps proposing points near the same boundary, so the same bracket is updated over and over, progress stalls, and the iteration limit is exceeded.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
